title: The Slave and the Lion
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Slave ran away from his master, by whom he had been most cruelly treated, and, in order to avoid capture, betook himself into the desert. As he wandered about in search of food and shelter, he came to a cave, which he entered and found to be unoccupied. Really, however, it was a Lion's den, and almost immediately, to the horror of the wretched fugitive, the Lion himself appeared.

The man gave himself up for lost: but, to his utter astonishment, the Lion, instead of springing upon him and devouring him, came and fawned upon him, at the same time whining and lifting up his paw. Observing it to be much swollen and inflamed, he examined it and found a large thorn embedded in the ball of the foot. He accordingly removed it and dressed the wound as well as he could: and in course of time it healed up completely.

The Lion's gratitude was unbounded; he looked upon the man as his friend, and they shared the cave for some time together. A day came, however, when the Slave began to long for the society of his fellow-men, and he bade farewell to the Lion and returned to the town.

Here he was presently recognised and carried off in chains to his former master, who resolved to make an example of him, and ordered that he should be thrown to the beasts at the next public spectacle in the theatre.

On the fatal day the beasts were loosed into the arena, and among the rest a Lion of huge bulk and ferocious aspect; and then the wretched Slave was cast in among them. What was the amazement of the spectators, when the Lion after one glance bounded up to him and lay down at his feet with every expression of affection and delight! It was his old friend of the cave!
The audience clamoured that the Slave's life should be spared: and the governor of the town, marvelling at such gratitude and fidelity in a beast, decreed that both should receive their liberty.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Slave run away from his master?
options: Because his master could no longer feed him
Because he was sold to a new owner
Because he had been most cruelly treated
Because he wanted to explore the desert

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Slave find inside the cave he enters?
options: A Lion
A store of food left by hunters
Nothing at all, just empty rock
Another fugitive hiding there

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Slave discover wrong with the Lion's paw?
options: A deep cut from a hunter's trap
A broken claw causing pain
A snake bite near the toes
A large thorn embedded in the ball of the foot

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Slave eventually leave the cave and the Lion?
options: The Lion asks him to leave
He begins to long for the society of his fellow-men
The cave becomes too small for them both
He runs out of food to share with the Lion

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Slave once he returns to the town?
options: He is welcomed and given a new home
He is arrested for a crime he did not commit
He is recognised and carried off in chains to his former master
He is mistaken for someone else entirely

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what punishment does the master order for the Slave?
options: To be thrown to the beasts at a public spectacle
To be whipped in front of the town
To be sold to a distant land
To be locked away for the rest of his life

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Lion in the arena do when he sees the Slave?
options: He roars and charges at the crowd instead
He ignores the Slave and attacks another animal
He waits quietly at the edge of the arena
He bounds up to him and lies down at his feet with affection

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the governor decree at the end?
options: That the Slave should be freed but the Lion killed
That both the Slave and the Lion should receive their liberty
That the Slave should serve a new master instead
That the fight should continue the following day

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Lion behave so gently toward the Slave in the cave despite being a wild animal?
options: He mistakes the Slave for another lion
He has been tamed by hunters before this meeting
He is in pain from the thorn and seeking help rather than looking for prey
He recognizes the Slave from an earlier encounter

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the passage?
options: A kindness shown to a suffering creature can be repaid when least expected
Wild animals can never truly be trusted, even after help is given
Masters are always right to punish a runaway slave severely
Public spectacles were the safest way to test a criminal's guilt

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Slave go to avoid capture after running away?
options: Across the sea
Into a nearby forest
Up into the mountains
Into the desert

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Lion first approach the Slave in the cave?
options: By roaring loudly to frighten him
By fawning upon him and lifting up his paw
By circling him slowly at a distance
By blocking the entrance to the cave

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do the spectators react when they see the Lion approach the Slave gently?
options: With cheers of celebration
With complete silence
With amazement
With anger at the Lion's behavior

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the audience call for the Slave's life to be spared?
options: They are moved by the loyalty the Lion shows toward him
They believe the master's original punishment was unjust from the start
They want to see the Lion fight a different opponent instead
They recognize the Slave as an innocent man wrongly accused

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the years the Slave and Lion spent sharing the cave matter later in the arena?
options: The Lion had already forgotten the Slave by the time of the spectacle
The governor learns about their friendship beforehand and stages the scene
The Lion in the arena turns out to be a different lion entirely
That earlier bond is what makes the Lion recognize and spare him among the beasts

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "unbounded" mean in "The Lion's gratitude was unbounded"?
options: Quickly forgotten
Without limit
Difficult to notice
Shared unequally

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A slave is killed by a lion he had never met before
A lion helps a slave escape from his cruel master entirely
A slave who once helped a wounded lion is spared when that same lion recognizes him in the arena
A governor orders both the slave and the lion to be executed
